title: Birmingham 2022 Pre-Games Evaluation
file_title: Birmingham 2022 pre-Games evaluation framework and baseline report
description: The Birmingham 2022 Commonwealth Games Evaluation Framework Report, prepared by KPMG for the DCMS, outlines a comprehensive approach to assess the Games' economic, social, and environmental impacts, with a focus on diversity, inclusion, and sustainability. The evaluation, structured in three phases, employs a methodology based on the HM Treasury Magenta Book, including theories of change, stakeholder engagement, and a variety of data collection methods. It aims to measure the Games' legacy in terms of job creation, skills development, infrastructure, and community benefits, using 188 indicators to attribute outcomes to the Games. The report acknowledges challenges such as COVID-19 and Brexit in isolating the Games' effects and emphasizes the importance of accurate data collection and analysis. The evaluation will produce reports at three intervals post-Games to ensure accountability, transparency, and informed future mega event planning.

title: Broadband Connection Voucher Scheme
file_title: Broadband Connection Voucher Scheme Impact and Benefits Study
description: This document describes an evaluation of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport's Super Connected Cities Programme's Broadband Connection Voucher Scheme, which aimed to enhance economic growth by subsidizing the cost of improved broadband connections for small businesses. The evaluation used an impact study approach, revealing that over 54,000 small firms received grants, with 42,500 firms upgrading their internet connections to services that were, on average, 18 times faster. The results indicated that the UK gained at least £8 for every £1 spent on the scheme, with businesses reporting increased efficiency, profitability, and employment. The scheme also fostered competition and consumer choice by supporting hundreds of suppliers, particularly smaller ones, and group schemes were successful in improving connectivity in areas with poor service. The main conclusion is that the Broadband Connection Voucher Scheme significantly benefited participating businesses and the broader UK economy.

title: Covid-19 Loneliness Fund: A Process Evaluation
file_title: Covid-19 Loneliness Fund evaluation
description: This document summarizes evaluations of programs designed to combat loneliness during the Covid-19 pandemic, with a focus on the Covid-19 Loneliness Fund. The evaluations used a mix of literature reviews, data analysis, focus groups, and interviews to assess the effectiveness of services provided to various demographics, including women, younger adults, ethnic minorities, and people with disabilities. Key findings across the evaluations indicate that services such as befriending and digital inclusion programs were effective in reducing loneliness, though challenges such as digital exclusion and the need for sustainable solutions were noted. The evaluations also highlighted the impact of health status on loneliness, showing that those with long-term illnesses or disabilities experienced higher levels of social isolation. Overall, the programs had a positive impact, but recommendations for future interventions include allowing more setup time and considering the effectiveness of digital versus in-person delivery.

title: Cyber Discovery Evaluation
file_title: CyberFirst Evaluation (PDF version)
description: The document provides an evaluation of the Cyber Discovery programme, a component of the UK's National Cyber Security Strategy designed to develop cyber security skills among 14 to 18-year-olds, with a particular focus on increasing female and ethnic minority participation. The evaluation, carried out by Ecorys and the University of Kent, employed a mixed-methods approach, including surveys, interviews, and case studies. Findings suggest that the programme is successful in engaging participants and enhancing their skills in computer science and cyber security, although it does not significantly increase interest in cyber security careers. The programme exceeded its participation targets and improved diversity. Feedback from Club Leaders and industry experts was generally positive, recognizing the benefits for students and the industry. Challenges identified include the need for more guidance for less experienced students and the impact of COVID-19 on participation. Recommendations for the programme include promoting diversity, integrating career guidance, and providing better support for Club Leaders and students. The programme is acknowledged as a valuable initiative in addressing the cyber security skills gap and is advised to continue its development to fulfill this objective.

title: CyberFirst Evaluation
file_title: CyberFirst Evaluation (PDF version)
description: This document describes an evaluation of the CyberFirst program, designed to develop cyber security talent and increase diversity in the field. The program offers initiatives like summer courses and industry partnerships. Ecorys and the University of Kent used a mixed-methods approach to assess the program's effectiveness. Results show that participants, often with prior cyber experience, gained knowledge and skills, and were more likely to consider cyber security careers, although their interest in the field did not significantly increase. The evaluation suggests the need for more career guidance and diversity improvements. Separately, interviews with industry stakeholders affirm CyberFirst's role in diversifying the talent pool, especially among women, and in streamlining recruitment. The program is commended for preparing students for the workforce, but concerns about costs and retention were raised. Recommendations include enhancing accessibility, providing clear career pathways, and focusing on soft skills. The program is seen as successful in engaging participants and is advised to attract a wider socio-economic demographic while maintaining engaging content.

title: Evaluation of BDUK Gigabit Vouchers: Initial Impacts and Benefits
file_title: Evaluation of BDUK Gigabit Vouchers: Initial Impacts and Benefits
description: This document describes an evaluation of the BDUK Gigabit Vouchers program, which aims to enhance internet connectivity in the UK by subsidizing gigabit broadband installation for businesses. The program's objectives include improving digital literacy and helping businesses adapt to challenges like the COVID-19 pandemic. The evaluation used a variety of methods, including counterfactual analysis, business surveys, and statistical models, to measure the program's effectiveness. Results showed that the program increased the availability of ultra-fast broadband, especially in rural areas, and improved download speeds, although it did not significantly increase gigabit speed availability. The Rural Gigabit Connectivity scheme and project vouchers were more effective than the original scheme. Businesses reported benefits such as increased productivity and adaptability, with rural and smaller businesses experiencing transformational effects. While some challenges were noted, overall, the program had a positive impact on broadband performance and availability, leading to various business improvements. Further research is needed to understand the long-term impacts and rural spillover effects.

title: Evaluation of Gaming Machine (Circumstances of Use) (Amendment) Regulations 2015
file_title: Evaluation of Gaming Machine (Circumstances of Use)(Amendment) Regulations 2015
description: This document describes an evaluation of the Gaming Machine (Circumstances of Use) (Amendment) Regulations 2015, which aimed to help users of B2 gaming machines control their gambling by requiring higher stakes to be authorized by staff or through account-based play. The evaluation used empirical methods to analyze gaming behavior, including account usage, stake patterns, and session durations. Results indicated a decrease in bets over £50 and an increase in bets in the £40-£50 range, suggesting a shift in staking behavior possibly due to the regulations. The impact on industry revenue was significant, with estimates of a decrease between £66m and £78m. The evaluation found that while the regulations have led to some changes in player behavior, the uptake of verified accounts was low, and the long-term effects on player control and industry profits are still uncertain. Further research is needed to fully understand the impact of the regulations.

description: This document describes an evaluation of the Audio Content Fund (ACF), a pilot program launched in 2019 to enhance the UK's public service audio content by supporting independent audio producers and promoting diversity in broadcasting. Employing a theory-based methodology, including surveys and interviews, the evaluation found that the ACF met all eight criteria set by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media & Sport, supported sector growth, and delivered high-quality content to a broad audience. Despite challenges like engaging unsuccessful bidders and assessing value for money, the ACF has been effective in job creation, nurturing new talent, and producing content reflective of the UK's diversity. The evaluation suggests future funding should prioritize education, collaborative efforts, and listener feedback, highlighting the ACF's transformative impact on the independent audio production sector and public service broadcasting.

title: Evaluation of the Coronavirus Community Support Fund Value for Money Report
description: This document describes an evaluation of the Coronavirus Community Support Fund (CCSF), which was designed to assist communities during the COVID-19 pandemic and prevent the closure of vital organizations. The evaluation, carried out by NPC and Ipsos MORI, employed a range of methodologies, including cost-benefit analysis, economy, and efficiency assessments, as well as regression analysis and surveys. The findings indicate that the CCSF delivered value for money, with benefits outweighing the costs and benefit-cost ratios suggesting economic and efficient use of funds. The CCSF was effective in meeting basic needs, increasing social contact, and reducing the demand for public services, which resulted in cost savings. Most grants were allocated to small organizations, helping them to continue operations during the crisis. Challenges faced during the evaluation included the diversity of grantees, the unique circumstances of the pandemic, and difficulties in measuring long-term effects. Despite these challenges, the CCSF was found to be equitable and effective, although the evaluation acknowledges the tentative nature of its conclusions and the importance of context in assessing economic impact.

title: Evaluation of the Culture Recovery Fund
file_title: Evaluation of the Cultural Recovery Fund
description: This document describes an evaluation of the Culture Recovery Fund (CRF), a UK initiative designed to support cultural organizations during the COVID-19 pandemic. The CRF aimed to ensure the survival and accessibility of over 5,000 organizations, with an emphasis on diversity and cultural access. A mixed-methods approach, including case studies, surveys, and econometric analysis, was used to assess the fund's effectiveness. The evaluation found that the CRF successfully helped organizations to survive, adapt, and reopen, supporting jobs and preserving cultural assets, while also delivering broader social and economic benefits. However, challenges were noted in targeting organizations at the highest risk of failure. The evaluation also reviewed changes in application processes by different funding bodies, noting a shift towards efficiency by the Arts Council England and increased detail and scrutiny by the National Lottery Heritage Fund and Historic England. Overall, the CRF was deemed efficient and potentially vital for the future of many organizations and jobs, with recommendations for future crisis support funds.

title: Evaluation of the DCMS 50+ Volunteering Programme
file_title: 50+ Volunteering Final Report
description: This document describes an evaluation of a 50+ volunteering programme managed by Nesta and the Centre for Ageing Better, which awarded £5.2 million to 39 organizations to engage individuals aged 50 and over in public service. Nottingham Trent University conducted the evaluation using a mixed-methods approach, assessing the programme's efficiency, effectiveness, and impact. The programme mobilized over 25,320 new volunteers and reached numerous beneficiaries, despite challenges such as volunteer engagement and innovation management. Key recommendations include fostering age-friendly volunteering and embedding evaluation into programme design. The programme's impact was somewhat limited by its post-start commissioning and the COVID-19 pandemic. Positive outcomes were noted for organizations, beneficiaries, and particularly for the 50+ volunteers who contributed significantly. The document also reviews specific initiatives like Grandmentors and Dance to Health, highlighting the benefits of volunteering for social connections, personal growth, and public service contributions, while emphasizing the need for tailored recruitment and inclusive practices to engage older volunteers effectively.

title: Evaluation of the Fast Track Digital Workforce Fund
description: This document describes an evaluation of the Fast Track Digital Workforce Fund, a program designed to mitigate digital skills shortages in Greater Manchester and Lancashire by promoting collaborations between training providers and employers. The program aimed to enhance employment opportunities, particularly for those in low-skilled positions or from underrepresented groups, and to improve productivity and services for employers. title: Evaluation of the Industrial Masters in AI (IMAI) Programme
file_title: IMAI Evaluation Report
description: This document summarizes the evaluation of two distinct programmes aimed at enhancing AI skills and recruitment opportunities in the UK. The first, the Industry-funded Masters in AI (IMAI) programme, delivered by the Institute of Coding, sought to provide AI master's places, work placements, and strengthen industry-higher education links. Despite not meeting its funding target and facing challenges like COVID-19, industry engagement, and data tracking, the programme was seen as a good investment with positive industry feedback. Recommendations include increasing awareness and mentorship, and exploring alternative funding. The second programme focuses on improving recruitment for industry partners, offering marketing benefits and promoting regional diversity by collaborating with northern English universities. It suggests a model with cohort learning, mentoring, flexible placements, and a reduction in administrative burdens for industry partners. It also recommends incorporating data science and AI conversion courses for efficiency. Success hinges on aligning delivery targets with objectives and thorough data collection for evaluation. Both programmes show potential for expanding AI skills development in the UK, with suggestions for enhancing effectiveness and sustainability.

title: Evaluation of the Libraries: Opportunities for Everyone Innovation Fund Executive Summary
file_title: Evaluation of the Libraries: Opportunities for Everyone innovation fund executive summary
description: This document describes an executive summary of the evaluation of the Libraries: Opportunities for Everyone (LOFE) innovation fund, which was part of the Libraries Deliver: Ambition for Public Libraries in England 2016-21 strategy. The fund, managed by the Arts Council, was launched in December 2016 to support projects aimed at benefiting disadvantaged people and places in England, with grants awarded to 30 projects across 46 library services. Traverse conducted the evaluation using a mixed-method approach, assessing the fund's impact on participants and communities, and the extent to which it met its objectives of reducing disadvantage through engaging activities and skill development. The evaluation found improvements in staff morale, service reach, and library environments, as well as positive effects on people's perceptions of libraries. Successful projects addressed aspects of disadvantage and developed innovative practices, with libraries using funding to support disadvantaged communities through technological resources and creating inclusive spaces. Challenges included securing staff support and engaging participants effectively. Recommendations from the evaluation include focusing on specific audiences and outcomes, embedding evaluation into projects, and encouraging partnerships with local organizations to enhance library services and reputation.

description: The interim report by ICF Consulting Services Limited evaluates the Life Chances Fund (LCF), a policy designed to support individuals facing societal barriers in England through Social Impact Bonds (SIBs). The LCF, initiated in 1969, aims to expand the SIB market and tackle complex social issues. The evaluation employed administrative data, interviews, and case studies to measure the fund's influence on the SIB market and its success in meeting its goals. Findings reveal some progress in project initiation and investment attraction, but also highlight difficulties such as stakeholder engagement, outcome measurement, and the inherent complexities of SIBs. Success factors include financial backing and collaborative efforts, while challenges involve securing stakeholder commitment and the risks associated with innovative methods. The report offers interim insights and recommendations for enhancing future funding programs, emphasizing the need for simplified processes and better support. The final evaluation is expected in 2020, with additional reports until 2025. The evaluation acknowledges the potential of SIBs for innovative funding and the importance of clear communication and process efficiency for their success.

title: Evaluation of the Taylor Review Pilot Emerging Monitoring and Evaluation Evidence: September 2018 to March 2019
file_title: Interim Evalution of the Taylor Review Pilot (Word)
description: This document describes an evaluation of the Taylor Review Pilot, a program designed to enhance the sustainability of Church of England church and cathedral buildings through increased community engagement and improved maintenance strategies. The pilot, which operated in Greater Manchester and Suffolk, provided support via workshops, a Minor Repair Grant Fund, and the assistance of Fabric Support Officers and Community Development Advisers. Frontier Economics employed a logic model approach to evaluate the program, examining inputs, activities, outputs, and early outcomes. The evaluation revealed that stakeholders valued the support from officers, though some aspects such as grant processing limited broader support capabilities. Challenges were encountered in engaging urban worship places, and the Minor Repair Grant Fund fell short of its target. Workshops were well-received but faced attendance barriers. The evaluation will continue post-March 2020 to fully assess the pilot's impact and inform future policy, emphasizing the importance of regular maintenance for the preservation of church buildings.

title: Evaluation of the economic impact and public value of the Superfast Broadband Programme
file_title: BDUK Superfast Evaluation Annex A: Reducing the Digital Divide
description: The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport conducted an evaluation of the Superfast Broadband Programme, which was launched to expand superfast broadband in the UK, particularly in underserved areas, with the goal of boosting productivity, employment, and quality of life. The programme successfully funded broadband for 4.8 million premises by December 2017, with a significant portion in rural regions. The evaluation, covering the period from June 2012 to June 2016, employed statistical analyses and surveys to measure the programme's impact on broadband access, economic growth, and wellbeing. Findings revealed that the programme substantially increased broadband access, with 2.5 million premises covered that would not have been otherwise, and expedited coverage for another 1 million. It also positively affected local economies, job creation, and wellbeing, though it did not significantly decrease economic inactivity among benefit claimants. The programme was efficient, reducing upgrade costs by 40% due to high take-up rates. The evaluation concluded that the programme was successful in extending broadband coverage and had the potential to further enhance quality of life, while also identifying areas for future research and policy improvement.

title: Impact Evaluation of the Coronavirus Community Support Fund
description: This document describes an evaluation of the Coronavirus Community Support Fund (CCSF) by Ipsos MORI, which aimed to assist small and medium-sized community organizations during the COVID-19 pandemic. The CCSF's goals were to support affected individuals and communities, prevent the closure of essential services, and promote volunteer involvement. The evaluation adhered to ISO 20252 standards and employed a Theory of Change, contribution analysis, surveys, interviews, and case studies to assess the program's impact. Key findings revealed that the CCSF helped organizations adapt and continue operations, reaching approximately 6.58 million beneficiaries, including those facing mental health challenges, disabilities, and financial difficulties, and involved around 183,200 volunteers, many of whom were new and from diverse backgrounds. The CCSF was found to be a significant financial contributor to positive outcomes, such as improved mental health and social contact, and was crucial in maintaining the financial health and capacity of organizations. While the impact on public services was less clear, the CCSF prevented many temporary closures. The evaluation highlighted the importance of rapid scoping, data collection, and high survey response rates, achieved by making participation a grant requirement. Future evaluations could benefit from direct beneficiary interviews and similar methodological approaches. Ipsos MORI's evaluation concluded that the CCSF was successful in increasing community support and suggests that future emergency funding programs could learn from this approach.

description: This document describes an interim evaluation of the Internet of Things (IoT) UK Research and Innovation Programme, which operated from 2015 to 2018 with the aim of fostering IoT development for economic and social benefits in the UK. The evaluation, carried out by SQW for the Department of Digital, Culture, Media & Sport, utilized a mixed-methods approach, including contribution analysis, case studies, and feedback from participants. Although the programme faced delays, budgetary issues, and had mixed success across projects, it has made significant progress and enhanced the UK's IoT profile. Some projects exceeded targets, while others encountered challenges such as recruitment and technical issues. The evaluation highlighted the need for better programme management and suggested improvements for future delivery, including enhanced monitoring and support for collaboration. Despite the challenges, the programme has begun to deliver tangible outcomes and is expected to have a lasting impact, though the full realization of its collaborative potential has yet to be achieved.

description: This document describes an evaluation of the Mobile Infrastructure Project (MIP) by the Department for Culture, Media, and Sport, aimed at enhancing mobile network coverage in rural UK areas. The evaluation used financial modeling, cost-benefit analysis, and surveys, revealing that the MIP successfully reduced the digital divide, supported economic growth, and improved public safety by delivering mobile connectivity to areas lacking coverage. The project exceeded expectations by building 75 masts at a cost 30% lower than anticipated for 60 masts, with a benefit to cost ratio of 0.73 over 20 years. The report also discusses the obligations of mobile operators, the viability of multi-user sites, and the potential underestimation of benefits due to not including long-term profits or higher willingness to pay for 3G/4G services. Annexes provide detailed data used in the analysis and case study requests to further demonstrate the project's impact.

The Programme successfully established consortia, developed testbeds, and delivered most use case trials, leading to increased R&D and improved perceptions of 5G. title: Tech City UK Impact Evaluation
file_title: Tech City UK Impact Evaluation (Word File)
description: The Tech City UK Impact Evaluation Final Report evaluates the effectiveness of Tech City UK (TCUK) and its associated programs in bolstering the UK's digital tech sector. TCUK's initiatives, including Future Fifty, Upscale, Northern Stars, the Digital Business Academy, and the Tech Nation Visa Scheme, aimed to support digital businesses and entrepreneurs, particularly in London and the North of England. The evaluation employed stakeholder feedback, interviews, surveys, and economic modeling to gauge the impact. Results showed that TCUK positively influenced networking, management skills, and company credibility, but had a limited effect on employment and sales turnover. The report estimated a gross value added of £11m to the UK economy and a benefit-cost ratio of 5.8:1, highlighting TCUK's role in advocacy and thought leadership. Recommendations for TCUK include focusing on a more balanced geographical activity, securing longer-term funding, and operational improvements. The report concludes that TCUK has contributed to the digital economy by enhancing connectivity, raising company profiles, and providing learning opportunities, but suggests that clearer strategic objectives and better program utilization could further improve its effectiveness.

title: What is the impact of social action befriending services at the end of life?
file_title: Evaluation of the End of Life Social Action Fund
description: This document describes an evaluation of various befriending service interventions aimed at improving the quality of life for individuals in their last year of life. The interventions, which were delivered by trained volunteers, sought to provide social support and companionship to reduce loneliness and enhance well-being. Methodologically, the evaluations employed a mix of quantitative and qualitative approaches, including randomized controlled trials, questionnaires, interviews, and validated scales such as the WHO QOL Bref and the De Jong Gierveld Loneliness Scale. Results across studies indicated a small but significant effect on the physical domain of quality of life, with certain demographics showing more pronounced benefits. While the interventions did not significantly improve overall quality of life or reduce loneliness, they did show a trend favoring the intervention and no evidence of harm. The evaluations concluded that volunteer services are valuable in providing compassionate support at the end of life, but larger trials and further research are needed to confirm findings and optimize service delivery. Additionally, the document discusses the importance of methodological rigor in palliative care research and the role of appendices in supporting the main content of scientific publications.

description: This document describes an evaluation of the Youth Engagement Fund (YEF), a £16m Payment by Results (PbR) program designed to prevent disadvantaged youth aged 14 to 17 from becoming NEET (Not in Education, Employment, or Training). The YEF aimed to support these individuals through various projects, test a PbR approach with social investors, and promote the social investment market. Ecorys UK conducted the evaluation using stakeholder consultations, case studies, and process evaluations. The findings indicated that while the program engaged young people and implemented interventions, it struggled to support the most disadvantaged and to address broader factors of youth unemployment. Outcomes were achieved in education, but sustained employment and higher qualifications were less successful. The Social Impact Bond (SIB) model was generally well-received, but recommendations were made for future programs to support younger individuals, provide more holistic support, and create more flexible payment structures. The evaluation also compared SIBs and PbR, with mixed views on their effectiveness. Key lessons for future NEET prevention programs and SIBs include the need for clear theories of change, contract management flexibility, and the application of learned lessons to enhance positive effects.
